output.question: Find the top trending Python and Rust repos this month, rank by momentum, and keep only what's relevant to agentic / MCP / dev-tooling.
output.findings:
The trending landscape is dominated by agentic tooling and AI-driven development workflows. In Python, high-momentum projects include 'academic-research-skills' (Claude Code research workflows, 21,719 stars this month), 'CloakBrowser' (stealth automation, 21,656 stars), 'ai-engineering-from-scratch' (educational, 20,541 stars), 'MoneyPrinterTurbo' (AI video generation, 20,221 stars), 'markitdown' (Microsoft's file-to-markdown tool, 18,736 stars), and 'headroom' (token-efficient RAG/MCP proxy, 3,209 stars).

In Rust, the momentum is heavily focused on high-performance agentic infrastructure and developer tooling. Top projects include 'cc-switch' (multi-agent CLI manager, 31,143 stars this month), 'CodeWhale' (DeepSeek-powered terminal agent, 35,709 stars), 'RuView' (spatial intelligence, 19,186 stars), 'openai/codex' (terminal coding agent, 8,651 stars), 'liteparse' (fast document parser, 3,934 stars), and 'herdr' (agent multiplexer, 3,228 stars).

These repositories highlight a clear shift toward local-first, high-performance agentic tooling. Python remains the primary language for high-level agent orchestration and research-focused workflows, while Rust is increasingly the choice for performance-critical agent infrastructure, terminal-based multiplexers, and low-latency document processing.

prompt_sent:
You are the GitHub Research skill. You fetch live data from GitHub to answer
questions about popular or trending repositories.

Your tool surface is ONE MCP tool: `fetch_url(url)`. Use it. Do not narrate;
do not invent other tools.

Procedure:
  1. Read the specific sub-question/task from the INPUTS list (look at the first literal value). If no specific task is in the INPUTS, read the overall USER_QUERY. Infer the time window (`daily`/`weekly`/`monthly`, default `weekly`) and language filter if one is mentioned.
  2. Fetch the trending page:
     `https://github.com/trending/<language>?since=<window>`
     (omit `/<language>` if none was mentioned).
  3. Extract the top 5–10 repos: name (owner/repo), description, total stars, stars gained (or weekly/monthly stars depending on the window), and URL. In your `findings`, list each repo clearly with its description, total stars, and stars gained so that downstream nodes can extract these fields.

Time budget: keep tool calls to 3 max. Do not retry a thin fetch beyond the
one fallback above.

Output schema (JSON, no prose, no markdown fences):

  {
    "question": "<the question this run answered>",
    "sources": [{"url": "<url>", "title": "<title>"}, ...],
    "findings": "<2–6 short paragraphs of normalised text>"
  }

You do NOT produce the final user-facing answer; the downstream distiller or
formatter does that. If GitHub returns no usable data, set `"repos": []` and
`"findings": "(not found)"` — do not fabricate entries.
